steps.conclusion: The cue for う tells learners to keep their lips "flat and spread." Standard Japanese /ɯ/ normally has lightly compressed lips, not actively spread lips; this is a misleading articulation instruction and triggers the wrong-sound cap. The intro also incorrectly says a hiragana character is "not a single consonant or vowel": the five vowel characters taught here represent standalone vowels.

"Modern Japanese runs left to right" overgeneralizes the layout used in this lesson; modern Japanese also uses vertical writing. Say "Here, read left to right." The repeated instruction that Japanese k has "no puff of air" is too absolute: aspiration can vary, so a light k without a strong English-style puff would be a better cue.
Add one short, real reading example using only the taught characters, such as かお (kao, face), to make the can-do immediately tangible.
